description: PV sizing model: roof geometry inference, azimuth production factors, plane solar score, flat-roof GCR, default panel specs, system losses, and HPXML roof plane extraction

reviews.title: Per-shape usable roof area fractions: Gable=0.75, Hip=0.35, Flat=0.70
reviews.prompt: The PV sizing model applies per-shape usable roof area fractions: Gable=0.75, Hip=0.35, Flat=0.70. These fractions account for fire-code setbacks (~15% perimeter reduction) and obstructions (~12% for vents, chimneys, skylights). Verify: (1) Fire-code setback of approximately 15% — is this based on IBC 2018/2021 Section 1204 requiring 3-foot setbacks on ridge and eaves? Different jurisdictions have different requirements; is 15% a conservative average? (2) Obstruction allowance of ~12% — does this match NREL rooftop PV potential methodology? NREL's PV Rooftop Potential study found obstruction losses of 10-18% depending on roof complexity. (3) The Hip fraction of 0.35 appears very low compared to Gable at 0.75. Hip roofs have more ridge/valley/hip lines that preclude panel placement, but a 0.35 multiplier implies only 35% of gross roof area is usable — is this physically justified or overly conservative? Compare against NREL SAM's PV rooftop shading and mounting methodology and the OCHRE PV.py roof area estimation. (4) For complex roofs (multiple dormers, varying pitch), do these single-fraction defaults adequately represent usable area, or should a more granular obstruction model be used? A systematic error in usable area fractions directly scales PV production estimates by the same proportion.

reviews.title: Azimuth production factor lookup table — South=1.0, East=0.80, North=0.45 at 45-degree snaps
reviews.prompt: The azimuth production factor lookup table maps cardinal and intercardinal directions to production multipliers: South=1.0, East=0.80, North=0.45 (at 45-degree snap intervals). Verify these values against NREL SAM azimuth derating factors or pvlib-python's azimuth loss model. Key checks: (1) Are these multipliers latitude-dependent? A north-facing panel at 25°N latitude (Miami) has a different relative production than at 48°N (Seattle). The lookup table appears to be latitude-independent — verify whether NREL SAM or PVWatts v5 applies a latitude correction to azimuth factors. (2) The 45-degree snap resolution means a panel at 22° east of south gets the same factor as one at 45° east of south. What is the maximum error introduced by this quantization? At mid-latitudes, a 20° azimuth error produces approximately 2-3% production error — is this acceptable for a sizing model? (3) East and West are symmetric (both 0.80) — does the afternoon temperature penalty make West slightly worse than East in reality? (4) Compare against the pvlib-python irradiance.transposition model and OCHRE PV.py orientation factors. (5) Verify that the lookup table interpolation (nearest-neighbor vs. linear) is documented and that edge cases (due North, due South exactly) produce consistent values.

reviews.title: Plane solar score: DIFFUSE_FRAC=0.18 and latitude exponent formula
reviews.prompt: The plane solar score calculation uses DIFFUSE_FRAC=0.18 as the diffuse fraction and a latitude exponent of 1.0 + 0.005 * (lat - 35). Verify: (1) Is DIFFUSE_FRAC=0.18 typical for middle latitudes? The actual annual-average diffuse fraction varies from ~0.25 (cloudy climates like Seattle) to ~0.12 (arid climates like Phoenix). A fixed 0.18 may be a reasonable continental-US average, but does HARES support climate-zone-specific diffuse fractions from TMY3 data? (2) The latitude exponent formula 1.0 + 0.005*(lat-35) provides a latitude roll-off for direct-beam availability. At latitude 45°N, the exponent is 1.05; at 25°N, it's 0.95. Verify that this linear roll-off matches the cosine-of-latitude relationship for annual beam irradiance. NREL data shows annual GHI changes by approximately 0.5-1.0% per degree of latitude in the continental US — does the 0.005/degree slope produce appropriate sensitivity? (3) The reference latitude of 35°N (roughly Oklahoma City/Albuquerque) — is this the correct anchor point for the continental US? (4) Compare against NREL SAM's plane-of-array irradiance model and PVWatts v5's transposition model for consistency. The plane solar score is a rough heuristic for PV production potential; document its accuracy bounds compared to full TMY3-based simulation.

reviews.title: Flat roof GCR latitude-dependent table (0.35/0.40/0.50)
reviews.prompt: The flat roof ground coverage ratio (GCR) uses a latitude-dependent lookup table with values 0.35, 0.40, and 0.50 across latitude bands. Verify: (1) GCR = module area / total roof area; for flat roofs with tilted racking, GCR is limited by row-to-row shading avoidance. At latitude 40°N with a 10° tilt, the minimum row spacing ratio is approximately 2.0-2.5, yielding GCR of 0.30-0.40. Do the HARES GCR values match this geometry? (2) Latitude band boundaries — verify that the latitude bands are correctly chosen to represent the transition from near-equatorial (tight spacing, high GCR) to high-latitude (wide spacing, low GCR) installations. (3) Commercial vs. residential flat roof assumptions — commercial flat roofs typically use 5-10° tilt with ballasted racking, while residential flat roofs may use steeper tilts. Does the GCR table assume commercial or residential typical values? (4) Compare against NREL SAM's GCR recommendations and the OCHRE PV.py flat roof model. An incorrect GCR directly scales the number of modules that can fit on a flat roof, linearly affecting total system capacity. (5) Is there an east-west oriented flat roof configuration (dual-tilt) considered, which would have a different GCR than south-facing tilted rows?

reviews.title: Default panel wattage 420W and area 2.0 m² — modern residential panel representation
reviews.prompt: The default PV panel is specified as 420W nameplate with 2.0 m² area, yielding 210 W/m² efficiency (21% module efficiency). Verify: (1) Does this represent a typical ~2024 residential panel? In 2024, mainstream residential panels range from 400-440W with areas of 1.8-2.2 m² (efficiency 20-22%), so 420W/2.0m² is a reasonable midpoint. However, for a model that may be used for 2030+ projections, should the default be forward-looking? (2) These defaults should be user-configurable from a defaults CSV or configuration file, not hardcoded. Verify whether the PV sizing module reads from hares-config defaults or uses these as compile-time constants. Hardcoded defaults prevent users from modeling specific panel makes and degrade over time as panel wattages increase. (3) Verify that the panel temperature coefficient (typically -0.3 to -0.4%/°C for silicon) is either included in the default system losses or applied explicitly in the production model. Without temperature derating, production will be overestimated in hot climates. (4) Compare against NREL SAM default module database and OCHRE PV.py default module parameters. (5) The panel area is used to compute how many panels fit on the usable roof area — verify that the packing efficiency (panel + inter-panel gap) is accounted for separately from the usable roof area fraction.

reviews.title: Default system losses fraction 0.14 — verify match to PVWatts v5 defaults
reviews.prompt: The default system losses fraction of 0.14 is stated to account for soiling (2%), mismatch (2%), wiring (2%), inverter (4%), and other losses (~4%). Verify that the total of 0.14 matches PVWatts v5 default loss assumptions: (1) PVWatts v5 default total system losses are 14.08%, broken down as: soiling 2%, shading 3%, snow 0%, mismatch 2%, wiring 2%, connections 0.5%, light-induced degradation 1.5%, nameplate rating 1%, age 0%, availability 3%. HARES's stated breakdown (2+2+2+4=10%) only accounts for 10 of the 14 percentage points — what are the remaining 4%? (2) The inverter efficiency loss of 4% appears low for modern string inverters (typical CEC efficiency 97-98%, implying 2-3% loss) but reasonable for microinverters or older central inverters. Verify that the source for the 4% inverter loss is documented. (3) Are system losses applied as a single lumped derate factor (Capacity * (1 - 0.14)), or are they broken out into separate AC and DC side losses? Lumped derating conflates temperature-dependent inverter losses with temperature-independent wiring losses. (4) Is there any latitude, climate, or roof-mount-type dependence in the system losses? For example, soiling losses are higher in arid regions, and snow losses are significant in northern climates (PVWatts v5 defaults snow=0% but notes region-specific values). (5) Compare against NREL SAM detailed loss model and PVWatts v5 documentation for consistency and traceability.

reviews.title: Roof shape inference logic — classification rules and false-negative risks
reviews.prompt: Roof shape is inferred from building metadata and roof plane geometry using classification rules: apartment → Flat, all-flat (all tilts < threshold) → Flat, 3+ distinct azimuths → Hip, tile/slate roofing material → Hip. Verify: (1) False negatives for hip roofs with only 2 recorded planes — many HPXML files record only two dominant roof planes even for hip roofs (e.g., north-facing and south-facing), omitting the smaller east/west hip planes. With only 2 planes, the algorithm would not trigger the 3+ azimuth rule and could misclassify a hip roof as gable. What is the expected misclassification rate based on HPXML data quality? (2) Tile/slate roofing material as a hip roof predictor — while tile and slate are more common on hip roofs (Mediterranean, Spanish Colonial styles), this is a probabilistic association, not a deterministic rule. Does this rule fire before or after the azimuth count rule? If tile+2 planes, does HARES classify as hip (via material) or gable (via insufficient azimuths)? (3) Apartment → Flat classification — multi-family buildings commonly have flat roofs, but not universally (townhouse-style apartments often have gable roofs). Is this rule based on building type or number of dwelling units? (4) Wrong shape classification propagates into the usable roof area fraction (Gable=0.75 vs. Hip=0.35 vs. Flat=0.70), so a hip misclassified as gable would overstate usable area by more than 2×. Verify that the classification is conservative (prefer lower usable fraction when uncertain). (5) Is there a user override mechanism to explicitly set roof shape when metadata is ambiguous or known to be wrong? Compare against OCHRE PV.py roof geometry inference for consistency.

reviews.title: HPXML building→RoofPlane extraction — tilt fallbacks, boundary wiring, area inheritance
reviews.prompt: HPXML building data is parsed into RoofPlane structures in hares-io. Verify the extraction logic: (1) Tilt fallbacks — when a roof plane in the HPXML file lacks an explicit tilt (RoofPitch element missing or zero), HARES falls back to tilt=0 (flat). Is this the correct default? Some HPXML generators omit tilt because it's implied by roof type (e.g., cathedral ceiling implies the roof pitch). A tilt=0 fallback could misclassify a sloped roof as flat, affecting the roof shape inference and GCR/usable area calculations downstream. (2) Boundary index wiring — HPXML roof planes reference boundary polygons (RoofBoundary elements) that define the 3D footprint. Verify that boundary vertex ordering is correctly preserved and that area is computed correctly from the polygon vertices (shoelace formula, accounting for coordinate system). (3) Area inheritance — when a roof plane does not have its own area element, does HARES compute area from the boundary polygon, inherit from the parent surface, or default to zero? An area=0 roof plane would silently exclude that plane from PV sizing. (4) Azimuth propagation — verify that the azimuth angle read from HPXML is correctly interpreted as degrees from true north (clockwise) and converted to the internal representation used by the azimuth LUT (which appears to use South=0 convention). A north-reference vs. south-reference confusion would swap azimuth factors and produce completely wrong production estimates. (5) Multi-building HPXML files — verify that roof planes are correctly associated with the correct building/dwelling unit and not cross-wired between units in multi-family HPXML files. Compare extraction logic against the HPXML v4.0 schema specification and OCHRE's HPXML parsing in Dwelling.py.
